items.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025
items.q: And then I played with Sharon Jones, the great singer that’s in her seventies.

ctx.x: Yeah. All right. I’ve got a question I’ve been working on and maybe you can help me actually just form it, but it seems that jazz has had differing and changing roles in society, if we think back in its very early days it was “new” music, then it became really high entertainment pop music, sort of in the swing era. In the ‘50s you had sort of bebop characters and the Dizzy Gillespie sort of persona. Some civil rights connections in the ‘60s. This is all my own opinion, but do you feel that jazz has a role in…

Yeah I think it has the role to tell the truth about, you know, the individual’s experience. The collective experience of, you know, whoever the artist is and where they are geographically, regionally, and also to be able to tell the story and have what you have to present be something that you can share with people. I think this music is a social music. It’s a music that’s meant to be, you know, played, for people, you know with people. And yeah I think that’s something that we can really benefit from in terms…

development, that’s all in this type of music. And also there are so many things that we can learn about it because it’s intergenerational. You know I could go and play with 15- year-olds. I played with a young tenor player last night named Emilio Modeste. I mean he’s the spitting image of — like I thought I was playing next to Wayne Shorter and he’s probably half my age. You know and then I played with Sharon Jones, the great singer that’s in her seventies. And so I think that aspect of it, the social aspect and…
